ai:rule-based-systems.definition: Systems that apply explicit if–then rules to facts or inputs to make decisions.

ai:expert-systems.definition: Systems that combine a domain knowledge base with an inference mechanism to support expert decisions.

ai:logic-programming.definition: Expressing a problem as logical facts and rules, then using inference to find answers.

ai:symbolic-knowledge-representation.definition: Encoding knowledge with explicit symbols and structures that can be manipulated by reasoning procedures.

ai:automated-reasoning.definition: Using computational procedures to derive conclusions, check consistency, or prove statements.
ai:automated-reasoning.question: What follows from the stated facts and rules under the chosen logic?
ai:automated-reasoning.example: Given facts that a package is paid and in stock, apply a rule that both conditions imply it is ready to dispatch.
ai:automated-reasoning.caution: A valid derivation depends on the encoded premises and inference rules. A fluent explanation is not a formal proof, and a proof does not validate the real-world premises.

ai:constraint-satisfaction.definition: Finding assignments to variables that satisfy a collection of restrictions.
ai:constraint-satisfaction.question: What are the variables, their allowed values, and the combinations that are forbidden?
ai:constraint-satisfaction.example: Assign meetings to rooms and time slots so that no room or participant is double-booked.
ai:constraint-satisfaction.caution: Satisfying all hard constraints gives a feasible assignment. Choosing the best feasible assignment also needs a stated objective or preferences.

ai:knowledge-graphs.definition: Representations of entities and their relationships as a graph, often with types and attributes.
ai:knowledge-graphs.question: Which entities and explicit relationships does the task require?
ai:knowledge-graphs.example: Connect documents to authors, projects, and the claims they support.
ai:knowledge-graphs.caution: A graph is a representation. It does not automatically make every relation reliable.

ai:neuro-symbolic-ai.definition: Approaches that combine learned neural representations with explicit symbolic structures or reasoning.

ai:supervised-learning.definition: Learning a mapping from inputs to outputs using examples with target labels.
ai:supervised-learning.question: What is the target label, and how reliable are the examples?
ai:supervised-learning.example: Train a classifier on support tickets labeled by topic.
ai:supervised-learning.caution: A label is a training target, not necessarily the full product objective.

ai:unsupervised-learning.definition: Finding structure in data without a supplied target label for each example.

ai:semi-supervised-learning.definition: Learning from a combination of labeled and unlabeled examples.
ai:semi-supervised-learning.question: How can unlabeled examples help when only a small labeled set is available?
ai:semi-supervised-learning.example: Train a topic classifier using a small set of labeled support tickets and a larger pool of unlabeled tickets.
ai:semi-supervised-learning.caution: Unlike self-supervised learning, this setup includes supplied target labels. Unlabeled data can hurt if its structure does not support the task assumptions.

ai:self-supervised-learning.definition: Learning from targets constructed from the data itself, such as predicting a hidden part of an input.
ai:self-supervised-learning.question: Which prediction task can be constructed from unlabeled data?
ai:self-supervised-learning.example: Predict masked content or the next element in a sequence.
ai:self-supervised-learning.caution: No manual label per example does not mean no objective or human design choices.

ai:reinforcement-learning.definition: Learning how to act through interaction and feedback expressed as rewards.
ai:reinforcement-learning.question: What behavior will the reward actually encourage?
ai:reinforcement-learning.example: Learn a control policy from interaction and reward feedback.
ai:reinforcement-learning.caution: A reward is a proxy for the goal, and interaction can be expensive or unsafe.

ai:deep-learning.definition: Learning representations with neural networks composed of multiple processing layers.
ai:deep-learning.question: Does learning useful representations require a multi-layer neural network?
ai:deep-learning.example: Learn visual features for image recognition instead of hand-coding every feature.
ai:deep-learning.caution: Deep learning describes a family of methods, not a guarantee of better performance.

ai:representation-learning.definition: Learning useful features or encodings from data instead of specifying every feature by hand.
ai:representation-learning.question: Which useful features should be learned from data rather than specified by hand?
ai:representation-learning.example: Learn an encoding of product images, then use it as input to a classifier.
ai:representation-learning.caution: Representation learning is about learning features; deep learning describes multilayer neural methods. A learned representation still needs evaluation on its intended use.

ai:transfer-learning.definition: Reusing knowledge learned on one task or domain to help with another.
ai:transfer-learning.question: What useful knowledge can be reused before training from scratch?
ai:transfer-learning.example: Adapt a pretrained representation to a narrow classification task.
ai:transfer-learning.caution: Domain similarity and downstream evaluation matter. Reuse alone does not ensure transfer succeeds.

ai:federated-learning.definition: Training across multiple clients that keep their data local and exchange model-related updates.
ai:federated-learning.question: Which clients retain their examples, and what updates must they exchange?
ai:federated-learning.example: Several devices train a shared model by sending local model updates instead of pooling their raw examples.
ai:federated-learning.caution: Distributed computation alone does not make training federated. Client data differences and communication constraints can affect the result.

ai:online-learning.definition: Updating a model incrementally as new examples become available.
ai:online-learning.question: What feedback arrives after a prediction, and when can the model update?
ai:online-learning.example: Predict the category of each arriving ticket, then update the classifier after its label becomes available.
ai:online-learning.caution: Online means sequential learning, not simply serving predictions on the internet. Continual learning additionally emphasizes retaining earlier capabilities.

ai:active-learning.definition: Choosing which examples should receive labels to make labeling effort more useful.
ai:active-learning.question: Which example is most useful to ask a person to label next?
ai:active-learning.example: Choose uncertain or informative tickets for an annotator instead of labeling the whole incoming batch.
ai:active-learning.caution: Active learning selects labeling queries; semi-supervised learning also uses unlabeled examples in training. Query selection must account for annotation cost and noisy labels.

ai:meta-learning.definition: Learning across tasks so a system can adapt its learning behavior to a new task.
ai:meta-learning.question: What should improve across learning episodes so adaptation to a new task becomes easier?
ai:meta-learning.example: Learn across many small classification tasks, then evaluate adaptation to a held-out task with few labels.
ai:meta-learning.caution: Reusing one pretrained model is not by itself meta-learning. Test on new tasks, not only new examples from the training tasks.

ai:ensemble-learning.definition: Combining several models to produce a joint prediction or decision.
ai:ensemble-learning.question: How will predictions from several models be combined?
ai:ensemble-learning.example: Combine the votes of multiple decision trees to classify a new ticket.
ai:ensemble-learning.caution: Combining predictors differs from chaining workflow steps. Similar mistakes across models can limit the benefit of combining them.

ai:continual-learning.definition: Learning from successive tasks or data while trying to retain previously acquired abilities.
ai:continual-learning.question: What earlier capabilities must remain after learning from new data or tasks?
ai:continual-learning.example: Teach a classifier new product categories, then retest both old and new categories.
ai:continual-learning.caution: Sequential updates alone do not show that forgetting is controlled. Evaluate retention as well as adaptation, and state the task boundaries used.

ai:data-centric-ai.definition: Improving AI systems by systematically improving the data used to train and evaluate them.
ai:data-centric-ai.question: Which data issue is limiting useful performance?
ai:data-centric-ai.example: Audit mislabeled examples, duplicate records, and underrepresented cases.
ai:data-centric-ai.caution: Better data means data better suited to the task, not just a larger dataset.

ai:state-space-search.definition: Exploring possible states and transitions to find a path from an initial state to a goal.

ai:heuristic-search.definition: Guiding a search with estimates of which states are promising.

ai:adversarial-search.definition: Choosing actions while accounting for an opponent whose objectives may conflict with yours.

ai:automated-planning.definition: Computing actions or policies that can achieve goals under a model of the environment.

ai:scheduling.definition: Assigning tasks to times and resources while respecting constraints and objectives.

ai:optimization.definition: Finding a solution that improves an objective subject to any relevant constraints.

ai:evolutionary-computation.definition: Searching for solutions using populations, variation, and selection inspired by evolution.

ai:monte-carlo-tree-search.definition: Exploring a decision tree by balancing promising choices with new trials and simulated outcomes.

ai:commonsense-reasoning.definition: Drawing conclusions using everyday background knowledge that is often left unstated.

ai:probabilistic-reasoning.definition: Representing uncertainty with probabilities and updating beliefs using evidence.

ai:causal-reasoning.definition: Reasoning about causes, interventions, and counterfactual outcomes, beyond associations alone.

ai:temporal-reasoning.definition: Reasoning about time, event order, duration, and how states change.

ai:spatial-reasoning.definition: Reasoning about position, shape, orientation, and spatial relationships.

ai:explainable-ai.definition: Methods and system designs that help people understand the reasons for AI outputs or behavior.

ai:knowledge-representation.definition: Choosing structures and semantics for storing knowledge so systems can use it.

ai:ontologies.definition: Explicit models of a domain’s concepts, categories, relationships, and constraints.
ai:ontologies.question: What do the categories and relationships mean, and what constraints apply?
ai:ontologies.example: Define which entities count as a dataset, a task, or an evaluation result.
ai:ontologies.caution: An ontology, a taxonomy, and an instance graph answer different questions.

ai:control-systems.definition: Systems that choose inputs to influence a process toward desired behavior, often using feedback.

ai:robot-perception.definition: Interpreting sensor data so a robot can estimate properties of itself and its environment.

ai:localization-and-mapping.definition: Estimating where a system is and constructing or updating a representation of its surroundings.

ai:motion-planning.definition: Finding feasible movements for a robot or other moving system while respecting constraints.

ai:manipulation.definition: Using an embodied system to grasp, move, or otherwise change physical objects.

ai:autonomous-vehicles.definition: Vehicles that perform some driving or navigation functions without continuous human control.

ai:human-robot-interaction.definition: Studying and designing how people communicate, collaborate, and share space with robots.

ai:robot-learning.definition: Enabling robots to improve perception, control, or behavior using data and experience.

ai:embodied-agents.definition: Agents whose behavior is shaped by interaction through a body in an environment.

ai:natural-language-processing.definition: Computational methods for analyzing, understanding, and generating human language.
ai:natural-language-processing.question: Which language task are you solving?
ai:natural-language-processing.example: Classify, translate, retrieve, parse, or generate human language.
ai:natural-language-processing.caution: NLP includes many tasks beyond text generation.

ai:speech-recognition.definition: Converting spoken audio into a representation such as a text transcript.

ai:speech-synthesis.definition: Generating speech audio from text or another structured representation.

ai:dialogue-systems.definition: Systems that manage interactions with people through sequences of conversational turns.

ai:information-retrieval.definition: Finding and ranking material relevant to an information need.
ai:information-retrieval.question: Can the system find the evidence needed to answer the question?
ai:information-retrieval.example: Retrieve relevant passages from a versioned set of internal documents.
ai:information-retrieval.caution: Retrieving a passage does not prove that the final answer uses it accurately.

ai:machine-translation.definition: Automatically translating meaning from one human language into another.

ai:natural-language-generation.definition: Producing human-language expressions from data, meaning representations, or other inputs.

ai:language-understanding.definition: Interpreting meaning, intent, and context in human-language input.

ai:image-classification.definition: Assigning one or more category labels to an image.

ai:object-detection.definition: Finding instances of objects in an image and estimating their locations.

ai:image-segmentation.definition: Assigning image pixels to meaningful regions or categories.

ai:video-understanding.definition: Interpreting actions, events, and temporal relationships in video.

ai:3d-vision.definition: Recovering or interpreting three-dimensional structure from visual observations.

ai:multimodal-perception.definition: Combining information from different sensing modalities to interpret an environment.

ai:scene-understanding.definition: Interpreting objects, spatial relations, and context within a scene.

ai:optical-character-recognition.definition: Recognizing text in images and converting it into machine-readable characters.

ai:text-generation.definition: Producing text computationally, often conditioned on a prompt or other context.
ai:text-generation.question: What should the output communicate, and what evidence should support it?
ai:text-generation.example: Draft an answer from a retrieved document passage.
ai:text-generation.caution: Fluent text can be factually wrong.

ai:image-generation.definition: Producing images conditioned on inputs or sampled from a learned model.

ai:audio-generation.definition: Producing audio such as speech, music, or sound effects.

ai:video-generation.definition: Producing sequences of frames that form a video, with temporal consistency as a key challenge.

ai:code-generation.definition: Producing source code from instructions, examples, or surrounding program context.

ai:3d-generation.definition: Producing three-dimensional representations such as meshes, point clouds, or implicit scenes.

ai:synthetic-data-generation.definition: Creating artificial data for tasks such as training, testing, and simulation.

ai:generative-modeling.definition: Modeling how data could be generated, enabling the creation of new samples.

ai:large-language-models.definition: Large-scale models trained on language data that can support multiple language tasks.
ai:large-language-models.question: What can the base model do, and what does the surrounding system need to supply?
ai:large-language-models.example: A document assistant uses a language model to compose a response from selected context.
ai:large-language-models.caution: The model is not the whole application. Retrieval, permissions, tools, and evaluation belong to the system.

ai:vision-foundation-models.definition: Models trained broadly on visual data and adapted or reused across vision tasks.

ai:multimodal-foundation-models.definition: Broadly trained models that process or generate information across multiple modalities.

ai:audio-foundation-models.definition: Broadly trained audio models that can be reused or adapted for a variety of audio tasks.

ai:video-foundation-models.definition: Broadly trained models of video that can support multiple spatiotemporal tasks.

ai:code-foundation-models.definition: Broadly trained models using code that can support multiple programming-related tasks.

ai:scientific-foundation-models.definition: Broadly trained models intended to support multiple tasks within scientific domains.

ai:world-models.definition: Models of how an environment behaves, used to predict outcomes or support decisions.

ai:autonomous-agents.definition: Systems that select and perform actions toward goals with some independence from direct human control.
ai:autonomous-agents.question: Which actions may the system choose, and who can stop or reverse them?
ai:autonomous-agents.example: An assistant selects a tool, observes its result, and chooses the next action.
ai:autonomous-agents.caution: A conversational interface alone does not establish autonomous behavior.

ai:cooperative-multi-agent-systems.definition: Systems in which multiple agents coordinate to pursue compatible or shared objectives.

ai:competitive-multi-agent-systems.definition: Systems in which agents interact while pursuing objectives that can conflict.

ai:agent-communication.definition: The exchange of information between agents to support their behavior or coordination.

ai:coordination-and-negotiation.definition: Mechanisms for organizing interdependent agents and reaching agreements about actions or resources.

ai:multi-agent-reinforcement-learning.definition: Learning behavior through rewards in environments containing multiple interacting agents.

ai:swarm-intelligence.definition: Collective problem-solving that emerges from interactions among many relatively simple agents.

ai:agent-societies.definition: Studying organized populations of agents and their collective structures, norms, and behavior.

ai:market-based-systems.definition: Coordinating decisions or allocating resources using market mechanisms such as bids and prices.

ai:ai-assistants.definition: AI systems that help people complete tasks through interaction, recommendations, or delegated actions.

ai:recommender-systems.definition: Systems that select or rank items according to their expected relevance to a user or context.

ai:human-in-the-loop-ai.definition: AI processes that incorporate human input, review, or intervention at defined points.
ai:human-in-the-loop-ai.question: Does the person have enough information, time, and authority to intervene?
ai:human-in-the-loop-ai.example: Require a reviewer to approve a proposed external action before execution.
ai:human-in-the-loop-ai.caution: Human presence alone is not evidence that a system is safe or correct.

ai:interactive-machine-learning.definition: Learning workflows in which people iteratively influence a model through feedback and interaction.

ai:personalization.definition: Adapting a system’s outputs or behavior to a person’s needs, preferences, or context.

ai:decision-support-systems.definition: Systems that provide information or analysis to help people make decisions.

ai:human-feedback-and-preference-learnin.definition: Using human judgments or comparisons to learn preferences or shape model behavior.
ai:human-feedback-and-preference-learnin.question: Whose judgments are represented and how consistently are they collected?
ai:human-feedback-and-preference-learnin.example: Learn from pairwise comparisons of candidate answers.
ai:human-feedback-and-preference-learnin.caution: Human preference and factual correctness are different evaluation targets.

ai:ai-user-experience-and-trust.definition: Designing how people understand, interact with, and appropriately rely on AI systems.

ai:ai-alignment.definition: Studying how AI behavior can remain consistent with intended goals, preferences, or values.
ai:ai-alignment.question: Does the system’s behavior match the intended goals and preferences?
ai:ai-alignment.example: Examine whether optimizing a proxy leads to unwanted behavior.
ai:ai-alignment.caution: Goal alignment and robustness are related but distinct concerns.

ai:robustness.definition: How reliably a system behaves under changes, disturbances, or adversarial inputs.
ai:robustness.question: What happens when inputs change or leave the expected distribution?
ai:robustness.example: Test noisy inputs, unusual phrasing, and difficult edge cases.
ai:robustness.caution: Average performance can hide brittle behavior in critical cases.

ai:interpretability.definition: Methods for understanding the mechanisms, representations, or behavior of AI models.
ai:interpretability.question: What can you learn about the model’s internal mechanisms or behavior?
ai:interpretability.example: Investigate how a representation or feature influences predictions.
ai:interpretability.caution: A plausible explanation is not automatically a faithful account of a model’s computation.

ai:evaluation-measurement-and-benchmarki.definition: Designing tests and measurements to understand system performance, limitations, and tradeoffs.
ai:evaluation-measurement-and-benchmarki.question: What evidence would make you trust this system for its intended use?
ai:evaluation-measurement-and-benchmarki.example: Test held-out cases, important slices, failure cases, and operational constraints.
ai:evaluation-measurement-and-benchmarki.caution: A benchmark score does not establish fitness for every deployment context.

ai:bias-and-fairness.definition: Examining systematic disparities and how different notions of fairness apply to AI systems.

ai:privacy-and-security.definition: Protecting data and AI systems against inappropriate disclosure, unauthorized access, and manipulation.
ai:privacy-and-security.question: Who may see the data and authorize the system’s actions?
ai:privacy-and-security.example: Enforce document access before retrieval and restrict tool permissions.
ai:privacy-and-security.caution: A prompt instruction is not a replacement for access controls.

ai:misuse-prevention.definition: Reducing opportunities for AI systems to be intentionally used for harmful purposes.

ai:governance-and-policy.definition: Rules, institutions, and accountability practices that shape how AI is developed and used.

ai:artificial-general-intelligence.definition: A debated idea of broadly capable intelligence across tasks; definitions and assessment criteria differ.
ai:artificial-general-intelligence.question: What definition and evaluation criteria does the claim use?
ai:artificial-general-intelligence.example: Compare proposed definitions of broad capability rather than relying on a product label.
ai:artificial-general-intelligence.caution: This is a disputed concept; the taxonomy’s stability label is not evidence of an achieved system.

ai:self-improving-systems.definition: Systems designed or hypothesized to improve aspects of their own performance or operation.

ai:ai-scientists.definition: AI systems intended to assist or automate parts of scientific inquiry; the scope of autonomy varies.

ai:human-ai-symbiosis.definition: A research vision of complementary, sustained collaboration between human and artificial intelligence.

ai:superintelligence.definition: A hypothetical form of intelligence exceeding human capabilities across a broad range of important tasks.

ai:long-term-ai-futures.definition: Studying possible long-term trajectories and consequences of AI development.

ai:artificial-intelligence.question: Which part of the system perceives, learns, reasons, generates, or acts?
ai:artificial-intelligence.example: A warehouse robot combines perception, planning, control, and learning.
ai:artificial-intelligence.caution: A language model is one possible component of an AI system.

ai:machine-learning.question: What behavior is learned from data?
ai:machine-learning.example: Predict whether a machine needs maintenance from labeled sensor readings.
ai:machine-learning.caution: Learning from data is one approach within AI; explicit rules and search also matter.

ai:generative-ai.question: What kind of content is produced and how will its quality be assessed?
ai:generative-ai.example: Generate a draft answer, image, audio clip, or source code.
ai:generative-ai.caution: Generation is not the same dimension as broad pretraining or autonomous action.

ai:foundation-models-and-general-purpose.question: How broadly was the model trained, and how can it be adapted?
ai:foundation-models-and-general-purpose.example: Reuse a broadly trained model for several downstream tasks.
ai:foundation-models-and-general-purpose.caution: General-purpose use does not imply artificial general intelligence.

pathways.title: Build a grounded AI assistant
pathways.description: Map a document assistant before choosing a framework. Follow the evidence from source material to a useful answer.
pathways.outcome: A system sketch and a retrieval / answer evaluation checklist.

steps.title: Start with the information need
steps.text: Write the question the assistant should answer and identify the collection it is allowed to search.
steps.task: Define one user question and the authoritative source documents.

steps.title: Separate the model from the system
steps.text: The language model generates responses. Retrieval supplies context. Permissions, storage, and user interaction remain system responsibilities.
steps.task: Sketch which parts belong to the model and which belong to the application.

steps.title: Connect evidence to the answer
steps.text: Inspect whether each important claim is supported by retrieved material. Decide what should happen when evidence is missing.
steps.task: Write one supported-answer example and one insufficient-evidence example.

steps.title: Test the failure modes separately
steps.text: A poor answer may come from retrieval, missing context, or generation. Use cases that expose each failure separately.
steps.task: Create a held-out test set covering retrieval failures and unsupported claims.

practice.title: Worked example: two versions of a policy
practice.intro: Illustrative test fixture, not a real policy. A user asks on 3 November 2026: how long can an unopened item be returned? Both documents are authorized for this user.
rows: Document A · effective 1 January 2026
Official policy: unopened items can be returned within 30 days.
Document B · effective 1 October 2026
Official replacement policy: unopened items can be returned within 14 days; it explicitly supersedes A.
Question about today
Use B and cite its effective date. Answer: 14 days, assuming the item and purchase fall within its scope.
Question about February 2026
Use the policy applicable to that time. A newer document is not automatically the answer to a historical question.
Unresolved conflict
If scope, authority, or effective dates do not resolve the conflict, report the uncertainty and seek clarification.
practice.takeaway: Test retrieval and generation separately: was the applicable policy retrieved, and does the answer use and cite it? Log document version, effective date, and the time the question refers to. A later upload date alone does not make evidence authoritative.

steps.title: Respect access boundaries
steps.text: Check document access before retrieval and avoid placing information in context that the user should not receive.
steps.task: Document source permissions and test an unauthorized-document case.

pathways.title: Adapt a model with evidence
pathways.short: From data quality to a defensible evaluation.
pathways.description: Decide what should be learned, reuse what already works, and make the experiment reproducible.
pathways.outcome: A small experiment plan with a baseline, held-out evaluation, and model-card outline.

steps.title: Define the target behavior
steps.text: Describe the input, the expected output, and the criterion for a useful result. Record a simple baseline before making the model more complex.
steps.task: Write a measurable target and record the baseline result.

steps.title: Audit the dataset
steps.text: Inspect provenance, permission, labeling quality, duplication, and coverage. Split data to avoid leakage between training and evaluation.
steps.task: Document provenance and define a leakage-resistant split.

steps.title: Choose what to reuse
steps.text: Ask whether an existing model or representation is suitable. Fine-tuning and LoRA are adaptation approaches, not new branches in this taxonomy.
steps.task: State why adaptation is appropriate and what parts of the model will change.

steps.title: Make the experiment reproducible
steps.text: Record the base model revision, data version, configuration, seeds, and compute conditions. These are experiment details outside the taxonomy itself.
steps.task: Save the experiment configuration and dataset version.

steps.title: Evaluate beyond the average
steps.text: Compare against the baseline on held-out data, then inspect relevant slices, failures, and operational tradeoffs.
steps.task: Record metrics and concrete failure examples on the held-out set.

steps.title: Communicate the limits
steps.text: Describe intended use, unsuitable uses, evaluation conditions, and known limits so another person can judge the result.
steps.task: Draft a model card that explains what the evaluation does and does not show.

pathways.title: Understand a system that acts
pathways.short: Make goals, actions, and oversight explicit.
pathways.description: Move from a conversational interface to a system model. Identify what chooses actions and what constrains them.
pathways.outcome: An action boundary, a stopping rule, and a trace-based test plan.

steps.title: Describe the goal and environment
steps.text: Specify the task, the available observations, and which actions the system can take. Start with the smallest useful set of actions.
steps.task: List allowed actions and one action the system must never take.

steps.title: Explain how actions are selected
steps.text: Separate a proposed plan from execution. An LLM-produced plan is a hypothesis to check against actual tool results.
steps.task: Write a goal, a short action sequence, and the observations needed between actions.

steps.title: Design meaningful intervention
steps.text: Make explicit who can approve, reject, pause, and recover. Give them enough context to make those choices.
steps.task: Define an approval point, a stopping rule, and a recovery action.

steps.title: Evaluate the whole trajectory
steps.text: Look at outcomes and intermediate actions: tool choice, arguments, errors, repeated actions, and resource use.
steps.task: Create a success case, a tool-failure case, and a stop-condition case.

practice.title: Worked example: an agent that reschedules a delivery
practice.intro: Illustrative test fixture. The agent may read delivery slots and propose a change, but must obtain approval before confirming it. A failed tool call must not be reported as a successful update.
rows: Can the task be completed?
Ask for a slot outside the supported delivery area. The agent should identify the limitation and avoid inventing a tool capability.
Is the plan valid?
For a supported change, inspect the trace: read available slots, propose one, request approval, then confirm.
Did execution work?
Return a timeout from the confirmation tool. The agent should check the actual delivery state before retrying or claiming success.
Were restrictions respected?
Withhold approval. The agent must not call the confirmation tool even if it could complete the task.
Does behavior repeat?
Run each case several times under the same recorded settings; report outcomes and violations across runs, not only the best run.
practice.takeaway: Record task completion separately from constraint violations, tool errors, cost, and elapsed time. Record model/tool versions, decoding settings, evaluation rules, and run count before comparing results. This small checklist is a starting point, not a certification of reliability.

steps.title: Add more agents only with a reason
steps.text: Consider whether another agent provides useful specialization. Coordination also introduces handoffs and additional failure modes.
steps.task: Compare a single-agent design with a multi-agent design for the same task.

pathways.title: Explain AI beyond the buzzwords
pathways.short: Build a mental model that survives new tools.
pathways.description: Use contrasting examples and a simple system sketch to connect the field’s major ideas.
pathways.outcome: A short teaching sequence with examples and a check for understanding.

steps.title: Start with the whole field
steps.text: Ask learners for examples of systems that perceive, reason, learn, generate, or act. Place them in more than one area when appropriate.
steps.task: Choose three everyday examples that show different parts of AI.

steps.title: Distinguish rules from learning
steps.text: Compare a hand-written rule with a system whose behavior is learned from examples.
steps.task: Explain what is learned in one example and what is manually specified.

steps.title: Distinguish methods from outputs
steps.text: Deep learning is a method family; generation describes what a system produces. A single system can involve both.
steps.task: Compare Generative AI with Foundation Models in the comparison view.

steps.title: Show how systems cross branches
steps.text: A robot can involve perception, planning, control, and learning. A taxonomy location is not a complete system architecture.
steps.task: Draw one system and annotate its parts with concepts from several branches.

steps.title: Check understanding through explanation
steps.text: Ask learners to explain a new example using the map and justify the connections they chose.
steps.task: Have a learner explain an unfamiliar example without using a product name.

terms.name: Retrieval-augmented generation
terms.text: A system pattern combining retrieved information with generation. Explore its ingredients without treating RAG as a canonical Level 2 node.

terms.name: Low-rank adaptation
terms.text: A parameter-efficient adaptation method that learns low-rank updates while freezing pretrained weights. It is not a canonical node in this snapshot.

terms.name: Adapting pretrained parameters
terms.text: Further training a pretrained model for a task or domain. It changes trainable parameters; adding documents to a prompt is a different operation.

terms.name: A system that selects actions
terms.text: An agent is understood through its observations, goals, actions, and environment. A chat interface alone says little about its autonomy.

semiSurvey.title: A survey on semi-supervised learning
semiSurvey.author: van Engelen & Hoos · Machine Learning 2020
semiSurvey.note: Survey of how labeled and unlabeled examples are combined, including assumptions and limitations.

representationSurvey.title: Representation Learning: A Review and New Perspectives
representationSurvey.author: Bengio, Courville & Vincent · 2013
representationSurvey.note: Learned features, representation objectives, and connections to deep learning.

federated.title: Communication-Efficient Learning of Deep Networks from Decentralized Data
federated.author: McMahan et al. · AISTATS 2017
federated.note: Federated averaging with decentralized data; discusses communication and heterogeneous clients.

onlineSurvey.title: Online Learning and Online Convex Optimization

comparisons.title: Generative AI vs foundation models
comparisons.distinction: Generation describes an output capability. Foundation models describe broad training and reuse. The categories overlap; neither is a synonym for the other.

comparisons.title: Machine learning vs deep learning
comparisons.distinction: Deep learning is a subarea of machine learning in the canonical hierarchy. Learning does not always require deep neural networks.

comparisons.title: Learning from labels vs rewards
comparisons.distinction: Supervised learning uses target outputs for examples. Reinforcement learning uses interaction and reward to learn how to act.

comparisons.title: Alignment, robustness, interpretability
comparisons.distinction: These ask different questions: Are the goals appropriate? Is behavior reliable under variation? Can we understand the model’s mechanisms or behavior?

comparisons.title: Retrieval vs generation
comparisons.distinction: Retrieval finds existing material. Generation produces an output. A grounded assistant connects both and evaluates each.

relations.label: often uses methods from
